This result is attained by analyzing a Plateau-type problem featuring a free boundary, defined both on the obstacle and at infinity, to determine the first obstacle-specific term (termed the {\it isoperimetric residue}) in the energy expansion as $v\to\infty$. A fundamental instrument in this analysis is a novel mesoscale flatness criterion for hypersurfaces with bounded mean curvature, developed by extending concepts from the theory of minimal surfaces with isolated singularities. iller-modified polymer matrices hold significant promise for enhancing the safety of high-risk engineering structures. These materials possess an inherent self-sensing capability, as their electrical conductivity alters in response to deformation and damage. This phenomenon, termed piezoresistivity, has been widely utilized for damage detection through electrical resistance measurements and tomographic imaging methods like electrical impedance tomography (EIT). While these approaches are highly effective at identifying the existence of damage, they struggle to deliver accurate details regarding the damage's shape, dimensions, or underlying mechanism. This limitation is especially problematic for laminated composites, which are prone to complex failure modes such as delaminations that are challenging to identify. To address this, we introduce a novel method for precisely determining the shape and size of damage in self-sensing composites. Our approach combines a genetic algorithm with realistic physics-based damage models to reconstruct accurate damage geometry from conductivity variations captured via EIT. We experimentally validated this technique using carbon nanofiber (CNF)-reinforced glass fiber-reinforced polymer (GFRP) laminates, focusing on two specific damage mechanisms: through-holes and delaminations. The results demonstrate that this new method can accurately reconstruct multiple through-holes with radii as small as 1.19 mm and delaminations resulting from low-velocity impacts. These findings indicate that integrating piezoresistivity with conductivity-based spatial imaging and physics-based inversion strategies can enable composites to "see" damage with both good accuracy and a high level of detail. Consequently, this capability could significantly advance the fields of impact damage detection and automated health monitoring in composites.

However, existing approaches predominantly assume static graphs, a limitation that hinders performance in highly dynamic systems where connectivity structures are non-stationary and largely unobserved. The vast diversity of life has resulted in a wide array of locomotive designs and methods, with various creatures utilizing legs, wings, fins, and other mechanisms to traverse their environments. This report defines the movement of general biological species as biolocomotion and introduces a computational method to identify it within raw video footage. Crucially, the motion of biological entities navigating an environment can be modeled as a superposition of overall positional advancement and an asymmetric oscillatory pattern; this signature is notably absent in non-biological objects in motion. By leveraging this characteristic signature alongside the distinction between an object's global movement (extrinsic motion) and the localized movement of its parts (intrinsic motion), we developed an algorithm to measure these traits in tracked objects to determine if they represent a biological entity in locomotion. Additionally, an alternative algorithm based on generic features and machine learning, assembled from related research areas, is presented for comparative analysis. The study provides a novel dataset of biolocomotion featuring a broad spectrum of biological and non-biological objects in natural settings, along with annotations for an existing camouflage animal dataset. Quantitative results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly outperforms the alternative approach, validating the hypothesis that biolocomotion can be reliably detected through its unique signature of positional advance with asymmetric oscillation and the disparity between extrinsic and intrinsic motion. Furthermore, the findings indicate that combining multiple related signatures yields more effective algorithms for identifying animals in video data. This work contributes a new dataset, algorithm, and validation framework to advance research into the automatic detection of animals camouflaged within their surroundings. The dataset is available at https://www.cse.unr.edu/~omoung99/locomotion.zip, and the code can be accessed at https://github.com/omounes/Biolocomotion-Detection-Algo. Consequently, there has been significant research into fast, approximate iterative methods for matrix inversion accelerated by Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), offering viable alternatives where traditional direct inversion methods are too costly. Existing techniques include the Neumann Series (NS), Newton iteration (NI), Chebyshev Iteration (CI), and Successive Over-Relaxation. This study introduces a novel iterative algorithm derived from the NS, termed "Nested Neumann" (NN). This approach generalizes higher-order iterations of NI and CI by leveraging a computationally efficient iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, dependent on a specified "inception depth." Mathematical analysis confirms that the NN method: (i) converges provided the preconditioning matrix satisfies the spectral norm condition required for NS, (ii) achieves a convergence rate equivalent to an order of (inception depth plus one), and (iii) performs optimally with an inception depth of one or two, contingent upon available RAM. Additionally, we derive an explicit formula for NN suitable for massive sparse matrices, accounting for increased computational costs. Crucially, we establish an analytical equivalence between NS and NN (including NI, CI, and higher orders), a finding particularly relevant for mMIMO systems. Finally, the NN method is applicable to positive semi-definite matrices for inversion and can be utilized for any linear system, whether sparse, dense, underdetermined, or overdetermined. Performance evaluations of NN across various scenarios are presented in the final section. Mathematical insights and simulation results indicate that NN is highly effective, often requiring less computation than NI and CI while delivering identical performance. Furthermore, its suitability for sparse matrices and systems with more variables than equations suggests broad applicability in performance-critical fields such as communications, statistics, machine learning, and engineering.

In this study, we investigate the topological and localization characteristics of a one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model featuring spatially correlated random binary disorder. Our findings reveal that such binary disorder can trigger a transition from a trivial insulator to a topological Anderson insulator across multiple parameter regimes. These topological Anderson insulators are identified by a disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states, observable via the inverse participation ratio in both real and momentum spaces. Furthermore, the boundaries of the topological phases align with analytical predictions derived from the self-consistent Born approach and the localization length of zero-energy modes. Ultimately, this work extends the concept of topological Anderson insulators to scenarios involving correlated disorders.

This paper addresses a distributed memoryless contextual linear bandit learning scenario where agents observe contexts and select actions, yet are geographically separated from the central learner who performs the optimization without direct access to the contexts. Assuming contexts follow a specific distribution, we introduce a method requiring approximately $5d$ bits per context when the distribution is unknown, and zero bits per context if it is known. This approach achieves a regret bound nearly identical to that of a fully observable setting. Specifically, the bound for the unknown distribution case improves upon existing results by a $\log(T)$ factor (where $T$ is the time horizon), while the bound for the known distribution case reaches information-theoretic tightness. Our proof technique for the unknown distribution case relies on a novel application of "covering" theory within bandit learning, a approach original to this work. The results indicate that the proposed framework achieves comparable performance costs to the standard "covering" method while reducing communication overhead by two orders of magnitude.

F) analyses and extremal network theory, this research investigates the maximum performance improvement of optimal power control compared to binary (on/off) strategies within large-scale interference networks to derive novel theoretical insights. Although numerical evidence suggests that binary power control is nearly optimal in most practical scenarios, this extremal analysis reveals that significant gains from optimal control can exist in specific settings, while also establishing GDoF-based bounds for these maximum gains. The study's primary contribution is the explicit characterization of the extremal GDoF gain of optimal power control over binary control as $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ for any number of users $K$. Specifically, this gain is bounded between $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ and $2.5\sqrt{K}$. For networks with $K=2,3,4,5,6$ users, the exact extremal gains are determined to be $1, 3/2, 2, 9/4$, and $41/16$, respectively. Networks achieving these extremal gains can be viewed as multi-tier heterogeneous systems. It is important to note that since the focus is on GDoF, these results hold asymptotically as node locations and channel realizations approach their extremal configurations; consequently, the actual bits-per-second performance improvement of optimal power control over binary control may be considerably smaller in real-world, finite-speed networks. To support these findings, simulation results are presented that align with the theoretical framework. The paper further explores generalizations regarding the typical gain range of optimal power control versus binary control, observations on the scalability of this extremal gain with $K$, and potential extensions to asynchronous networks and those employing time division multiple access.

Because the time step necessary to resolve collision dynamics is significantly smaller than that required for fluid flow, the computational expense of using the traditional soft-sphere model—which mandates such small steps—becomes prohibitive for simulations involving thousands of particles. While existing state-of-the-art methods artificially stretch the collision time to match several flow solver time steps, this approach introduces non-physical artifacts that compromise simulation results. In contrast, the proposed MTSA employs distinct time steps to independently resolve fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. The algorithm was evaluated against both particle-wall and particle-particle collisions, with optimal substep iterations determined to achieve excellent alignment between experimental data and results from the traditional soft-sphere model. Subsequently, the MTSA was applied to a sediment transport simulation (turbulent flow over an erodible bed) involving thousands of particles. Comparisons with the collision time stretching method revealed that the latter reduces particle stiffness, diminishes particle entrainment, and distorts turbulence and particle statistics. Ultimately, the MTSA achieved a computational cost reduction of approximately one order of magnitude compared to the traditional soft-sphere model while maintaining nearly identical accuracy. This significant decrease in expense without sacrificing precision represents the first demonstration of the feasible high-fidelity tracking of particle collisions without artificial time step stretching. The MTSA thus establishes a substantial advantage for future particle-resolved studies, particularly in scenarios where collisions are critical. OpenCFD has released the current 2D version of the algorithm under the MIT license.

Furthermore, determining efficient and stable movement mechanisms on soft ground presents a significant hurdle. This study aims to control a one-dimensional monopod hopper to achieve a target jump height. To accomplish this, I first established and validated a discrete element method (DEM) simulation environment featuring spherical granular material as the soft ground. Using this setup, I developed ground reaction force models based on resistive force theory (RFT). These RFT models were then employed to create a feedforward force control system for the robot. Within the DEM simulation, a feedback control loop was implemented to correct deviations between the actual ground reaction forces and the RFT predictions. Consequently, the robot successfully tracked desired trajectories and reached the target height within five hops, significantly reducing apex position errors compared to using feedforward control alone. Additionally, the experiment varied the robot's square foot area from 1cm² to 49cm². The results demonstrate that the feedback controller effectively manages fluctuations in ground reaction forces, even when the foot dimensions are comparable to the size of individual grains. However, very small feet (1cm x 1cm) proved challenging to control. These findings indicate that the feedback controller is highly effective in most scenarios, but further research is needed to extend these results to robots with smaller feet operating on stiffer grounds.

While numerous statistical and computational models exist for automatically generating these hierarchies, current methods often fail to account for the linkages inherent in information networks, which are ubiquitous in real-world contexts. Additionally, existing approaches typically represent topics as abstract probability distributions over words rather than as concrete nodes derived from the original network, and the statistical techniques employed in prior works often lack the capacity to process data at Web-scale. This paper introduces the Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), which leverages a distributed vertex-programming process to compute a nonparametric Bayesian generative model. Experimental results on three medium-sized datasets and the complete Wikipedia dataset demonstrate that HDTM is capable of inferring accurate hierarchies even when applied to large-scale information networks. Furthermore, the study utilizes real-world datasets to illustrate how computational algorithms can exploit the structural properties of information networks to aid in the automatic organization of knowledge. Beyond its novel approach to hierarchy inference, HDTM offers several advancements over prior work, including the integration of an information network into a Dirichlet Process framework, the utilization of Gibbs sampling for parameter estimation, and the implementation of vectorized code for processing large-scale datasets. The proposed method outperforms baseline algorithms in accuracy metrics and produces high-quality hierarchies when applied to Wikipedia, as verified by multiple evaluation measures. Consequently, HDTM serves as a robust tool for analyzing medium-to-large-scale datasets and effectively infers accurate and meaningful hierarchies from them. By leveraging structural insights from information networks, this model assists in organizing related entities into coherent knowledge systems. The source code for HDTM is accessible at https://github.com/aminpour/HDTM. Annealing involves slowly varying Hamiltonian parameters to explore equilibrium phases, making it a powerful method for solving complex optimization tasks. Conversely, quenches entail sudden Hamiltonian changes that drive the system into a non-equilibrium state. This study examines the connection between these two approaches, demonstrating that the critical bottleneck of quantum annealing—the minimum of the annealing gap—can be identified through a dynamical quench parameter characterizing the post-quench quantum state. By integrating statistical methods, such as neural network training, with quench data, we can reconstruct the complete functional behavior of the annealing gap. We further show that insights gained regarding the annealing gap, either partially or fully, enable the design of optimized quantum annealing protocols, yielding practical improvements in time-to-solution. These findings are based on simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians, which model challenging instances of the exact cover problem. Our results indicate that state-of-the-performance quantum annealing can be achieved by combining a finite number of quenches with a significantly larger thermal bath entropy than currently feasible on actual devices. Additionally, we outline how these strategies can be applied to discover fundamental properties of known or hypothetical materials, specifically the annealing gap, using near-term quantum annealers.

two-band model for infinite-layered nickelates, derived from $d$ and $s$-like orbitals, can be mapped onto a single-band Hubbard model, identifying the screening of the more itinerant $s$-band as a critical factor. Without screening, a strongly correlated band yields an antiferromagnetic ground state. Under weak screening, strong correlations drive electrons out of the $s$-band, resulting in an undoped Mott insulator with half-filled $d$ orbitals; this scenario contrasts with high-$T_c$ cuprate observations and suggests $s$-wave pairing for the superconducting state. Conversely, strong screening leads to partially filled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands that couple weakly, resembling a self-doped $d$ band with tendencies toward $d$-wave pairing. Specifically, in the strong screening regime, mapping to a one-band model reveals interesting spectral weight transfers when a second $s$ band is also partially occupied. Consequently, we conclude that both one-band physics and a Kondo-lattice-like regime arise from the same two-orbital model, contingent upon the strength of electronic correlations and the size of the $s$-band pocket. These findings underscore the importance of $s$-band screening and indicate that a straightforward explanation of nickelate $T_c$ using a two-band model is unattainable without additional structural or chemical complexity. Ultimately, we advocate for caution in drawing definitive conclusions about the underlying mechanisms of high-$T_c$ superconductivity based solely on simplified two-band models. Our results also address recent spectral weight transfer measurements and angular resolution $ARPES$ data, demonstrating that such phenomena are consistent with a two-band framework. However, we note that the experimental indication of a large $s$-band is subject to interpretation and could potentially arise from other mechanisms. Finally, we discuss the suitability of the two-band model in capturing the electronic structure of other layered nickelates. This work emphasizes that while a generic two-band model can account for various experimental findings, it fails to explain an $T_c$ as high as $42K$ in $\text{La}_{3}\text{Ni}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$. We explicitly contrast our approach with prior studies on nickelate electronic structure and highlight key differences between our model's predictions and those derived from angular momentum projected $d$-orbitals alone.

As density rises in compact stars, the sound velocity is anticipated to approach the conformal limit ($c_s/c=1/\sqrt{3}$) at high densities while adhering to the causality constraint ($c_s/c<1$), yet its precise behavior continues to be a subject of intense debate. It has been proposed that the sound velocity serves as a key indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, implying a specific functional form for its density dependence. This study investigates the general characteristics of the sound velocity and adiabatic index across hybrid stars, neutron stars, and quark stars, employing various conditions for the hadron-quark phase transition with differing interface tensions. Our findings indicate that the anticipated sound velocity behavior can also arise from the nonperturbative properties of the quark phase, independent of a deconfinement transition, resulting in more compact stars with comparable masses. Consequently, we introduce a novel class of quark star equations of state that could be validated by future high-precision radius measurements of pulsar-like objects. Specifically, a central sound velocity exceeding $0.7$c in quark stars is linked to a specific maximum mass of $M_{max}\simeq(2.05\pm0.02)n_\odot$. The derived general features of the sound velocity and adiabatic index can guide the development of quark star equations of state, which remain relevant to the high-density physics inherent to neutron stars. Moreover, the object's compactness is strongly correlated with its maximum mass when the central sound velocity is restricted to $c_s/c<0.8$. We conclude that the term "cross over" regarding the deconfinement phase transition in compact stars may be misleading, and the concept of a universal quark star relation between radius and mass remains unattainable. Signatures of the deconfinement phase transition in quark stars are most readily detected through the distinct slopes in the mass-radius relation that occur before and after the transition sets in. This approach can help elucidate the nature of the phase transition from future high-precision data on the compactness or mass-radius relations of quark stars. Consequently, the thermodynamic properties of quark matter at nuclear saturation density can be determined by combining observational data with QCD-based hadron interaction models. While the VSI generates turbulence characterized by vigorous vertical motions that can influence dust accumulation and settling, dust evolution itself can suppress this instability. Specifically, as dust grows and settles, it depletes the gas, rendering cooling inefficient in the optically thin outer regions. This study employs linear analysis to quantify how dust evolution stabilizes the VSI. We developed a cooling timescale model incorporating dust growth beyond micron scales and size-dependent settling. By integrating this model with linear stability analysis, we identified the "VSI zone" and calculated the maximum growth rate at various radial distances. Our results indicate that both dust growth and settling restrict the VSI zone to the immediate vicinity of the midplane. Consequently, the instability's growth rate diminishes because the vertical shear of rotational velocity—the instability's driving force—is weaker at lower altitudes. In our default model of a 0.01 solar mass disk, dust growth from 10 microns to 1 mm reduces the growth rate by a factor exceeding 10. Ultimately, the suppression of VSI-driven turbulence by dust evolution could accelerate further dust processing in outer disk regions and account for the significant dust settling observed in the HL Tau system. The VSI zone in our models aligns well with observations from the [^13]CO line in the TW Hara system, suggesting that dust evolution could drive other cooling-dependent instabilities, such as the magnetorotational instability, in outer disk regions.

We establish a Liouville theorem without relying on gradient estimates, demonstrating that any bounded harmonic function must be constant on such solitons. As a consequence, we prove that the dimension of the space of harmonic functions exhibiting polynomial growth is finite. Furthermore, we show that every polynomial growth harmonic function on a Ricci soliton with bounded geometry can be extended to a slightly larger manifold. Finally, we consider complete gradient Ricci solitons possessing two distinct points with identical potential functions, establishing that the dimension of polynomial growth harmonic functions remains finite under these conditions. This final result also applies to gradient shrinking Ricci solitons that are not isometric to the Gaussian soliton. These findings extend previous work by Cabezas-Apelmat and Xin (2019), which was limited to bounded harmonic functions on gradient K\"ahler Ricci solitons with constant scalar curvature. Additionally, our approach differs significantly from the method used by Cabezas-Apelmat and Xin (2019), as we do not employ maximal principle arguments via pseudo-distance; instead, we apply the positive mass theorem for Ricci solitons developed by Cabezas-Apelmat and Xin (2021). To achieve this, we first establish the positive mass theorem for gradient shrinking Ricci solitons within the context of polynomial growth harmonic functions and subsequently derive a weighted harmonic function version of the monotonicity formula found in [10].

These attacks conceal a secret function within a neural network that activates only when a specific trigger is present in the input. While most existing literature assumes static triggers with fixed locations and patterns—properties upon which many detection mechanisms rely—recent studies have demonstrated that image classification countermeasures like Neural Cleanse and ABS can be circumvented using dynamic triggers that remain effective regardless of their position or appearance. However, such dynamic backdoors are resource-intensive, typically requiring a significant portion of poisoned training data. This work presents the first demonstration that dynamic backdoor attacks can occur via a global average pooling layer without needing an increased volume of poisoned data. Despite this theoretical possibility, experimental results across sound classification, text sentiment analysis, and image classification indicate that implementing such attacks remains highly challenging in practice. To our knowledge, this research is the initial exploration of global average pooling-based dynamic backdoor attacks. We release our dataset and code for others to further investigate this area.

light propagation models grounded in the parametrised post-Newtonian (PPN) formalism, a framework designed to test potential deviations from general relativity. Among these effects, the post-Newtonian parameter $\gamma$, which quantifies gravitational light deflection, significantly influences astrometric data. This study analytically and numerically investigates how deviations of $\gamma$ from its general relativity value of unity impact parallax measurements in Gaia-like systems. Analytical calculations determined the changes in observable quantities resulting from minor variations in PPN $\gamma$, while numerical simulations were conducted to verify how these observable shifts translate into parallax estimation errors. The results indicate that a deviation in $\gamma$ causes a global parallax shift; a corresponding formula for this bias was derived, incorporating the satellite's barycentric distance, the angle between the spin axis and the Sun, and the uncertainty in $\gamma$. Numerical simulations of astrometric solutions corroborate these theoretical findings. Current estimates of PPN $\gamma$ suggest that the contribution to the Gaia parallax zero point is unlikely to exceed 0.2 $\mu$as. Furthermore, simulations reveal a strong dependence of the parallax shift on ecliptic latitude, an effect attributed to an asymmetry in the Gaia scanning law. This conclusion is fully supported by additional simulations utilizing a reversed precession direction for the spin axis relative to the Sun. We also examine the determination of this position-dependent parallax shift and its implications for the mission's scientific objectives. Although the simulations regarding the ecliptic latitude-dependent parallax shift are based on the approximation that the spin axis remains fixed throughout the observation period—a model that does not accurately reflect Gaia's actual scanning law—these results are directly applicable to Gaia data. The findings at other ecliptic latitudes can be explained by combining our results with the established effect of the PPN parameter $\gamma$ on parallax, such as near the ecliptic plane where the latitude-dependent shift vanishes. Our numerical demonstration of the latitude-dependent parallax shift was previously identified in literature but without an explicit explanation. While the magnitude of this shift is not unprecedented, its asymmetric nature distinguishes it from other relativistic parallax effects, including those arising from the combined influence of two identical mirrors in astrometric instruments or the Earth's orbital eccentricity. answering questions requiring commonsense background is common practice, yet it risks introducing noise and misleading data due to the vastness of available information. To address the challenge of effectively integrating relevant knowledge, we introduce a semantic-driven, knowledge-aware Question Answering framework that regulates knowledge injection through a coarse-to-fine approach. This framework employs a tailoring strategy to filter extracted knowledge based on the coarse semantics of the query during the extraction phase. Additionally, we developed a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that leverages structural knowledge to hierarchically fuse appropriate information according to the fine-grained semantics of the questions. Experimental results on the CommonsenseQA dataset show that our proposed method outperforms strong baseline approaches. Furthermore, case studies offer insights into the coarse-to-fine knowledge injection process and its positive impact on answering commonsense queries. The proposed framework is inherently extensible, capable of adapting to different knowledge bases and question answering tasks with minimal modification costs. The system source code is available at https://github.com/AhmedShakir99/SEM-KNOWQA.

Multi-document question answering (MDQA) combines information from various sources to respond to complex queries, but existing methods often fail to extract relevant knowledge due to noisy backgrounds and the lack of structural semantic understanding. To address these issues, we introduce a novel framework that incorporates knowledge graph (KG) into a multi-document QA setting by leveraging both textual knowledge and structural knowledge. We trained a BERT-based entity link module to incorporate textual knowledge and employed a graph attention network for fusion, utilizing the KG's structural information. Experimental results on the FlaviQA benchmark indicate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art models. Additionally, we released a new evaluation dataset named CORDMQA to further assess the performance of MDQA systems. Case study analyses demonstrate the effectiveness of each module within our framework. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/AhmedShakir99/SEM-KNOWQA.

Question answering with knowledge graphs (KGQA) has been extensively researched, yet most existing methods focus solely on symbolic knowledge, neglecting rich contextual information from unstructured text. To bridge this gap, we present a text-enhanced knowledge graph question answering framework (TE-KGQA) that leverages both symbolic and textual knowledge. We begin by introducing text-based relation extraction to enrich the KG with contextual data. Furthermore, a text-based attention fusion module utilizes the structural semantics of the knowledge graph to selectively integrate relevant textual information for semantic encoding. These cations generally exhibit brighter electronic emissions at longer wavelengths compared to their neutral counterparts. A comprehensive grasp of their near-UV to visible characteristics would enable their use as probes for local plasma conditions or as tracers for neutral gas within cometary systems. However, constructing complete spectral models for small, oxygen-containing molecular cations remains unfeasible due to current limitations in available molecular data. While the five simplest species—H₂O⁺, CO₂⁺, CO⁺, OH⁺, and O₂⁺—are well-characterized in certain spectral regions, they lack robust reference data in others. These knowledge gaps impede the creation of fully quantitative models of cometary spectra, specifically hindering accurate assessments of physical-chemical processes derived from the most prevalent cometary molecules. This work compiles existing spectral data for these species and identifies critical areas requiring future research, particularly where data scarcity significantly limits our understanding of cometary evolution. By leveraging the updated dataset, we propose novel references for CO⁺ and O₂⁺ and emphasize the urgent need for a detailed O⁺ spectrum. We conclude by outlining the spectral regions that remain poorly documented for these molecules and suggest utilizing the upcoming ESA comet mission, Rosetta/Philae, to gather necessary data. Ultimately, acquiring complete spectra for these molecular cations is essential for advancing our ability to interpret the rich emissions observed in cometary atmospheres and tails.

Solar flare classifications based on their hard X-ray spectra are integral to both observational analysis and theoretical modeling of these high-energy events. While the classically recognized classes A–R were established over four decades ago, recent analyses of data from the Fermi/GBM instrument suggest the existence of even more powerful flares, potentially exceeding class R. This study presents updated classifications for solar flare hard X-rays that incorporate these super-R class events. The proposed scheme relies on the time evolution of the primary thick-target electron spectrum, specifically its spectral index and high-energy cutoff, rather than the complexity of the resulting hard X-ray spectra. Consequently, this approach aligns with the general principles of solar flare modeling. Although the resulting classes may not be directly comparable to those from other classification methods—such as gamma-rays, radio emissions, or solar mass ejections—their ease of derivation from remotely observable quantities makes them practical for comparative analyses with other flare characteristics. PS) learning a model from data distributed across graph nodes, with Federated Learning (FL) serving as the primary application. A significant hurdle in FL is the communication bottleneck between nodes and the PS. Although performing multiple local updates per iteration before syncing with the PS is a common strategy to alleviate this bottleneck, the statistical heterogeneity of node-specific data often results in biased models and delayed convergence. To overcome both communication and data heterogeneity issues, we investigate Random Walk (RW) learning algorithms. These algorithms utilize direct connections between nodes, which are typically more efficient than communicating with the PS. In this framework, the model acts as a "baton" passed iteratively to a neighboring node after each update. Designing effective RW algorithms is complicated by data heterogeneity and uncertainty regarding data distributions; ideally, nodes with more informative data should be visited more frequently. We formulate this as a sleeping multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem to develop a near-optimal node sampling strategy that minimizes gradient estimate variance and asymptotically approaches optimal sampling. Building on this, we propose an adaptive random walk learning algorithm and provide theoretical convergence guarantees. Our numerical experiments confirm these theoretical results and demonstrate that our algorithm surpasses existing random walk methods. Furthermore, we extend this work to generalize gradient descent algorithms using random walks in FL settings, establishing theoretical convergence rates for both data-independent and data-dependent sampling schemes. Finally, we introduce a block-iterating random walk algorithm, which outperforms standard RW algorithms in terms of convergence speed, particularly when blocks contain a large number of data points. Throughout these contributions, various sampling algorithms are evaluated through extensive numerical simulations and real-world experiments using a handwritten digit dataset. The core innovations of this paper are summarized as follows:
1. We formulate a motivation-driven node sampling problem suitable for random walk learning in data-heterogeneous FL environments and develop an optimal (near-optimal in practice) sampling algorithm. This algorithm exceeds the performance of several state-of-the-art random walk algorithms, including RWTorch and Stochastic Averaging.
2. We develop block-iterating random walk algorithms and prove their convergence rates, both for data-independent sampling and for schemes that adapt to data distribution without prior knowledge. These block-iterating algorithms converge significantly faster than other random walk algorithms, especially when local data batches are large.
3. We generalize our findings to other first-order optimization algorithms, illustrating how random walk sampling can be applied to construct iterative solvers for distributed optimization problems with data-heterogeneous batches.

Drawing on North Carolina court data from 1994 to 2009, this study assesses whether mandating mental health treatment as a condition of probation reduces the probability of future re-offending. By exploiting random variations in judge assignments, the analysis compares probationers ordered to undergo treatment against those who were not. The findings indicate that requiring treatment lowers the three-year recidivism rate by 5.6 percentage points, representing a 17 percent reduction. The impact is strongest in preventing future violent and property crimes, with effects intensifying over time following conviction. Furthermore, a cost-benefit analysis demonstrates that the reduction in crime generated by the treatment exceeds the expenses associated with providing it. jme models were utilized to examine heterogeneous treatment effects across various sub-populations. The paper concludes by discussing the findings' implications for policy and existing literature.

The objective is to estimate $E_G(\eta(\theta)) \equiv \eta_G$ using independent observations $Y_1, \dots, Y_n$, given that $Y_i \sim f(y|\theta_i)$ and $\theta_i \sim G$ are independent and identically distributed. Notably, we show that certain instances of GMLE correspond to the non-parametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) for an unspecified distribution function; leveraging this, we derive convergence rates for $\eta_G$ within the broader class of distribution functions, generalizing earlier findings by Szabo (1984) and Juditsky and Zhang (2005). While deep learning techniques have recently advanced the field of Deep Learning-based Knowledge Tracing (DLKT), the underlying reasons for their success remain unclear, and rigorous evaluation of these methods remains difficult. First, existing data preprocessing steps are often proprietary and custom-tailored, hindering experimental standardization. Second, current DLKT studies frequently employ inconsistent evaluation protocols that lack alignment with real-world educational settings. To resolve these issues, we present \textsc{pyKT}, a comprehensive Python-based benchmark platform designed to ensure valid comparisons across DLKT methods through exhaustive evaluations. The \textsc{pyKT} library features standardized, integrated preprocessing procedures for seven popular datasets across various domains, along with implementations of ten frequently compared DLKT models to facilitate transparent experimentation. Our rigorous, fine-grained empirical studies reveal key insights for effective DLKT, such as how incorrect evaluation settings can cause label leakage and artificially inflate performance, and how many recent DLKT improvements are marginal compared to the initial model by Piech et al. \cite{piech2015deep}. We have open-sourced both \textsc{pyKT} and our experimental findings at https://pykt.org/, and we invite contributions from other research groups and practitioners. \textsc{pyKT} is also available on GitHub at https://github.com/zelyonky/pykt, HuggingFace at https://huggingface.co/zelyonky/PyKT, and Gitee at https://gitee.com/zelyonky/PyKT. We further discuss how \textsc{pyKT} can support future research questions, including the development of DLKT models optimized for data efficiency, privacy preservation, and cold-start scenarios.

The \textit{FedBuff} algorithm (Nguyen et al., 2022) mitigates this issue by enabling asynchronous updates that tolerate staleness, thereby improving training scalability while maintaining privacy through secure aggregation. This paper revisits the \textit{FedBuff} algorithm for asynchronous federated learning, extending prior analysis by eliminating boundedness constraints on the gradient norm. In this study, we explore transferring an English model to Czech ASR, a task involving languages with lower mutual intelligibility. This approach yields the corresponding covariant Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations for anisotropic conditions. Our findings regarding two-fluid configurations are presented across multiple figures and tables to ensure comprehensive understanding. Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) is essential for helping second-language learners refine their writing. While most existing studies assume access to abundant parallel data and adopt this premise, real-world L1 data is often limited. We evaluate various training strategies using a small L1 GEC dataset. Experiments demonstrate that meta-learning exceeds the cross-domain performance of other methods when only 200 parallel sentences are available. Additionally, we find that models trained on L1 data perform satisfactorily when fine-tuned on data from a different L1. As with other GEC tasks, the character-level approach proves most effective for this small L1 domain adaptation dataset. To facilitate further investigation, we have made the dataset and code publicly available. The dataset is hosted at https://osf.io/y583c/ and the code is found at https://github.com/zhengruic/GEC-L1-MLE.

among strategic agents with additive valuations, assuming no monetary transfers. In this context, a mechanism is an algorithm that processes agents' reported valuations rather than their true ones. Our primary objective is to determine if mechanisms exist that guarantee the existence of pure Nash equilibria for every scenario while simultaneously ensuring fairness in the resulting allocations. Specifically, we investigate two relaxations of envy-freeness: envy-freeness up to one good (EF1) and envy-freeness up to any good (EFX), ultimately providing an affirmative answer. We analyze two algorithms recognized for generating such allocations in non-strategic environments: Round-Robin, which yields EF1 allocations for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method by Plaut and Roughgarden [SIAM Journal of Discrete Mathematics, 2020] that produces EFX allocations for two agents. We demonstrate that all pure Nash equilibria of Round-Robin result in allocations that are EF1 relative to the agents' true values. Furthermore, we show that the Plaut and Roughgarden algorithm not only achieves EFX but also satisfies maximin share fairness in this strategic setting—a property it does not possess in the non-strategic case. Additionally, we prove that a weaker version of this result applies to any two-agent mechanism that consistently yields pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations. However, we also observe that neither algorithm necessarily leads to EF1 or EFX allocations in cases involving three or more agents. To our knowledge, this is the first study to establish the existence of EF1 and EFX allocations for algorithms designed for non-strategic agents within a game-theoretic framework. Our proofs rely on characterizing equilibria using the lens of matching theory and applying flow-based techniques. The flow-based approach not only affirms the fairness of outcomes in the two-agent scenario but also serves to characterize the limitations of generalizations to larger groups. While prior research has extensively analyzed the fairness of outcomes in equilibrium for envy-free allocation algorithms in non-strategic settings, our work is, to the best of our knowledge, the first to address this issue for strategic agents.

839 exhibits almost no star formation, except for a prominent complex of HII regions situated at the very edge of its outer disc. To investigate the origins and characteristics of this feature, researchers compared new Hα and archival broad-band imaging of UGC 8839 with similar data from four comparable spiral galaxies. The findings suggest that the off-axis star formation in UGC 8839 arises from a hyper-stable, dark matter-dominated disc throughout all radii, where the Toomre parameter reaches its lowest value only in the extreme outer disc. By employing analysis methods specifically tailored to handle the challenges of low surface brightness and small number statistics, the study determined that this HII region complex is not anomalous when modeled with a power-law luminosity function, indicating it is an intrinsic structure rather than a merging satellite. However, the entire population of HII regions in UGC 8839 demonstrates a distinct preference for larger galactocentric distances compared to those in the other sample galaxies. UGC 8839 vividly illustrates the connection between the baryonic-to-dark matter ratio and disc stability. Furthermore, a three-body interaction, resembling a scaled-down version of the mechanism thought to drive star formation in Malin 1, aligns with the observed extreme outer disc activity in UGC 8839's extended disc. A schematic diagram and the corresponding predictions regarding outer disc HII regions are presented. These results imply that the "missing" star formation in UGC 8839's outer disc has not vanished but has instead been transformed into a low-mass population of open clusters and ancient stellar populations, which are difficult to detect without specialized observations. These conclusions are drawn without relying on the assumption of equal prior probabilities for different star formation quenching scenarios. UGC 8839 serves as a prime target for deep imaging campaigns, and the derived lessons on outer disc interactions and star formation could significantly influence the evolution of future galactic superclusters. analyzing how mass accretion rates correlate with stellar and disk characteristics. While the scatter in these relationships can refine disk evolution models, this is only possible if accretion variability is properly considered. Although variability is significant during the embedded phases of star formation, it is often assumed to be minor in later stages. In this study, we report substantial accretion rate variations observed in the target XX Cha and discuss their implications for population studies of classical T Tauri stars. Comparing mass accretion rates derived from fitting UV-to-near-infrared spectra in recent X-Shooter observations with those measured 11 years prior using the same instrument, we find that XX Cha exhibits nearly 2 dex of accretion variability between 2010 and 2021. While the specific timescales of this variation remain uncertain, XX Cha demonstrates extreme accretion variability for a classical T Tauri star. If such behavior is common among these stars, potentially occurring on timescales longer than previously investigated, it could significantly influence disk evolution models constrained by the observed spread in accretion rates. Finally, we note that earlier studies relying on spectral lines to assess accretion variability may have underestimated the fluctuations in certain targets.

However, practical applications often involve behavior policies generating joint trajectories with varying performance levels; for instance, one agent might follow a random policy while others adhere to medium-quality policies. In cooperative games with global rewards, existing offline MARL approaches often allow agents to inherit these suboptimal random policies, thereby compromising the team's overall performance. This paper investigates offline MARL with explicit attention to the diversity of individual agent trajectories and introduces a novel framework termed Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) to mitigate this issue. Specifically, an attention-based reward decomposition network utilizes a differentiable key-value memory mechanism to assign credit to each agent in an offline setting. These decomposed credits facilitate the reconstruction of joint offline datasets into prioritized experience replay based on individual trajectories, enabling agents to share high-quality experiences. Subsequently, agents conservatively train their policies using a graph attention network (GAT)-based critic. Evaluations across discrete control environments (StarCraft II and multi-agent particle environments) and continuous control settings (multi-agent MuJoCo) demonstrate that our method yields significantly superior results on complex, mixed offline multi-agent datasets, particularly when there are substantial disparities in the quality of individual trajectories. This research offers an effective solution for leveraging shared offline datasets to enhance the performance of a new multi-agent system. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/zwzheng/SIT.

conference, Einstein proposed a thought experiment aimed at demonstrating the incompleteness of quantum mechanics by leveraging the instantaneous nonlocal consequences of wave function collapse—a phenomenon he termed "spooky action at a distance"—triggered by measurement. This event preceded the famous Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen critique. In this work, we utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous nonlocal nature of wave function collapse, combined with single-particle entanglement, generates the nonlocal effect known as steering. During this process, Bob's quantum state becomes contingent upon the specific observable Alice chooses to measure. To achieve this, we fully harness the spatial spreading of the single-particle's entangled wave function over large distances. Specifically, we show that the nonlocality inherent in single-particle entanglement enables the particle to "know" which detector Alice employs to steer Bob's state. Consequently, despite significant counterarguments, we establish that single-particle entanglement produces genuine nonlocal effects across distant locations, thereby opening avenues for implementing truly nonlocal tasks using this phenomenon. These findings highlight that single-particle entanglement can facilitate behaviors in real-world scenarios that would otherwise be impossible without nonlocal mechanisms. Furthermore, our results underscore that the magnitude of spatial entanglement, rather than the count of entangled particles, is the critical factor driving nonlocal effects in quantum mechanics. Finally, we demonstrate how, beyond the standard violations of Bell inequalities in multi-particle entanglement, single-particle entanglement can enable the "Teleporting of Time," where an event occurring now influences another event in a distant location that happened in the past. We conclude by discussing the implications of these findings for various fields, including teleportation, quantum computing, and causality. Our results indicate that single-particle entanglement can effect genuine nonlocal impacts, thereby expanding the practical applications of quantum mechanics beyond what is achievable with multi-particle entanglement alone. While we have long recognized that large spatial extensions create opportunities for nonlocal effects in multi-particle entangled systems, our analysis of the spatial distribution of single-particle entangled wave functions reveals that such effects are also possible with a single particle. This underscores that spatial entanglement, not multi-particle entanglement, is the fundamental source of nonlocality in quantum mechanics. advanced information technology systems has delivered substantial benefits to Internet of Vehicles (IoV) ecosystems, it has simultaneously amplified security and privacy risks. Consequently, privacy preservation methods have become a focal point in academic research to safeguard IoV data. However, these existing approaches require specific adaptations to align with evolving IoV architectures. Meanwhile, Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising solution for enhancing data privacy and security within IoVs. Concurrently, Blockchain technology offers significant potential through its secure, decentralized, and auditable mechanisms for data recording and sharing. This paper provides a comprehensive survey on the application and implementation of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs. Additionally, it examines potential challenges, proposed solutions, and future research directions associated with these frameworks. Ultimately, this survey serves as a foundational resource for developing modern Blockchain-Enabled FL solutions to address various data privacy issues and scenarios in IoVs. The proposed work is structured into five sections: an introduction, a literature review, discussions on challenges and future work, and conclusions. Keywords: Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning, IoV, Data Privacy and Security, Challenges, Future Work.

encoding framework grounded in Gaussian mixture models (GMMs). During the offline stage, the base station (BS) fits a GMM to uplink (UL) training data and subsequently generates a codebook in an unsupervised fashion by leveraging the model's clustering properties, assigning one codebook entry to each GMM component. In the online phase, the BS offloads the GMM to the mobile terminal (MT) without transferring the codebook; the MT then uses the GMM to identify the most appropriate codebook entry. This process eliminates the need for channel estimation at the MT, as it relies on the observed training sequence. The feedback transmitted to the BS comprises the GMM parameters and the index of the selected entry. Upon receiving this feedback, the BS executes a maximum likelihood decision to determine the exact spatial direction of the desired signal. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme outperforms existing codebook construction methods and achieves identical performance to a scenario with perfect feedback, all while significantly reducing feedback overhead compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, the online computational complexity at the MT is minimal, and the scheme requires no power loading during design since it is derived from the actual UL data distribution. Crucially, this method overcomes the limitations of traditional clustering-based codebook construction, which often fail to accurately capture complex data distributions; by utilizing a GMM, we achieve an accurate representation of the UL distribution for subsequent processing. The overall architecture offers several key advantages: (1) it bypasses the performance bottlenecks associated with standard codebook construction techniques, (2) it integrates offline design with low-complexity unsupervised learning, (3) it simultaneously exploits the spatial characteristics of the wireless channel and the non-Gaussian nature of the signal environment, (4) it avoids high feedback overhead by employing a compressed representation of the GMM, and (5) it necessitates no new hardware, making it readily deployable in practical systems. The core contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: (2) we propose a novel codebook construction scheme that leverages the GMM's superior clustering capabilities, and (3) we design a feedback structure that minimizes overhead while maintaining high feedback richness. The remainder of this work is organized into three additional sections. Section II details the system and signal models. Section III describes the proposed design structure, outlining the specific procedures for both the offline and online stages. Section IV presents simulation results and offers corresponding analyses. Finally, Section V concludes the paper.

investigate Population III (Pop III) binary remnant mergers within nuclear star clusters (NSCs) during the early stages of structure formation. We track the dynamical evolution of Pop III compact object binaries as cosmic structures develop, calculating how field stars' dynamical friction drives these remnants into NSCs. Subsequent evolution inside the clusters is modeled through three-body interactions and gravitational-wave (GW) emission. Our results indicate that 7.5% of Pop III binary remnants will migrate to the galactic centers (within 3 pc). Of these, approximately 5–50% will merge at redshifts greater than zero within NSCs, a process that includes systems with initially large separations (up to 1 pc). The merger rate density (MRD) reaches its peak at $z\sim 5-7$, ranging from $\sim 0.4-10\ \rm yr^{-1}\ \rm Gpc^{-3}$, which translates to a potential detection rate of $\sim 170-2700\ \rm yr^{-1}$ for third-generation GW detectors capable of observing up to $z\sim 10$. The majority ($\gtrsim 90\%$) of these mergers occur in low-mass ($\lesssim 10^{6}\ \rm M_{\odot}$) NSCs formed at high redshifts ($z\gtrsim 2$). While final mergers are primarily governed by three-body interactions, the MRD's uncertainty arises from uncertain input parameters, including the massive star wind model, rotational line damping, the initial binary separation distribution, and the Pop III stellar formation recipe. Systems with initial orbits exceeding the escape threshold (caused by supernova kicks exceeding the escape velocity) still manage to merge due to gravitational wave emission after dynamical hardening within the clusters. This population could comprise a significant fraction of the mergers detected by third-generation GW observatories in the high-redshift universe, potentially revealing physical properties of early galaxies that form heavy elements and constrain the cosmic metalenrichment history. Systems with initial orbits below the escape threshold experience complex dynamical evolution involving gas accretion, stellar interactions, GW emission, and possible supernova explosions; however, we currently lack the necessary observational constraints and theoretical models to incorporate these phenomena into our code. Future improvements incorporating these effects, along with better constraints on input parameters and a more comprehensive treatment of gravitational physics, could refine the predicted MRD. Our

Initially, the study focuses on a single-user, single-relay configuration, addressing a joint power optimization problem at the source and relay under individual power constraints for both nodes, with the goal of maximizing the end-to-end secrecy rate through optimal power allocation across sub-carriers. A joint optimization solution is derived using duality theory, where dual decomposition enables the application of convex optimization techniques to determine power loading at source and relay nodes. Simulation results are provided to validate the performance of the proposed schemes. However, existing systems are hindered by slow performance, limited to roughly 300 steps per second, primarily because of outdated infrastructure. We introduce TextWorldExpress, a high-performance framework implementing three standard text game benchmarks that boosts simulation speed by a factor of 1,000, achieving more than one million steps per second on standard desktops. Text-based games are a established method for testing models in artificial intelligence, enabling evaluation of agent performance in text-based question answering and strategy development without visual or auditory dependencies. Despite their utility, current benchmarks suffer from a severe performance bottleneck, restricting simulation speed to approximately 300 steps per second and making large-scale experiments impractical. In contrast, TextWorldExpress offers 1,000 times faster simulation, supporting modern agent training methods such as reinforcement learning. By utilizing the Numba compiler to convert Python code to C++, the framework achieves extreme performance while maintaining code clarity. It constructs performance-ready bytes quickly during game initialization and executes at near-native speed during play. Furthermore, the library includes 13 distinct games spanning various domains and difficulty levels, along with assessments across multiple metrics, ensuring it functions as a robust benchmark for evaluating models in text-based worlds. We released this framework to provide a simple, high-speed environment for building custom text-based games and a transparent benchmark for comparing performance across different models. Experiments confirm the framework's speed, achieving a maximum simulation rate of 1,310,000 steps per second. Code is available at https://github.com/tchennu/TextWorldExpress.

Text-based simulations offer a controlled setting for studying language models' common-sense reasoning and real-world problem solving. While previous benchmarks exist, their low execution speed limits the comparison of performance-heavy models like GPT-J and beyond. The TextWorldExpress framework resolves this speed issue

a potent class of deep neural networks extensively applied to sequence analysis and modeling. Nevertheless, their substantial model size hinders practical deployment, particularly in video recognition tasks involving high-dimensional data. To address this constraint and maximize the potential of LSTMs, this paper introduces an algorithm and hardware co-design strategy for high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, we introduce the FDHT-LSTM, a model based on a fully decomposed hierarchical Tucker (FDHT) structure that maintains high accuracy with ultra-low complexity. To leverage these algorithmic advantages, we designed a specialized hardware architecture capable of executing the FDHT-LSTM efficiently. Through a refined memory access scheme, the hardware supports complex matrix transformations in real-time without access conflicts. Evaluation results demonstrate that both the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the dedicated hardware accelerator deliver superior performance. Compared to state-of-the-art compressed LSTMs, FDHT-LSTM offers order-of-magnitude reductions in model size alongside significant accuracy gains across various video recognition datasets. Furthermore, against the state-of-the-art tensor decomposed hardware accelerator TIE, our FDHT-LSTM architecture achieves higher throughput, better area efficiency, and improved energy efficiency on the LSTM-Youtube workload. Similarly, on the LSTM-UCF workload, our design outperforms TIE in throughput and energy efficiency while maintaining comparable area efficiency. To validate the feasibility of this design, we provided comprehensive co-simulation results using the CSAM microarchitecture emulator and the NSys toolchain. To ensure broad applicability, we developed an open-source framework to automate the end-to-end design process for diverse workloads. This resource enables researchers to rapidly assess the efficacy of cutting-edge algorithmic methods for model compression and the hardware architectures required to deploy them. To showcase the framework's versatility, we also implemented a range of other state-of-the-art compressed LSTM algorithms. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ZeyuZhu/FDHTLSTM.

We introduce a related yet distinct proposal: the conjecture should instead apply to particles possessing non-negative self-binding energy. This perspective is especially significant in anti-de Sitter (AdS) space, as it admits a straightforward conformal field theory (CFT) dual. Specifically, if $\Delta(q)$ represents the scaling dimension of the lowest-dimension operator carrying charge $q$ under a global $U(1)$ symmetry, then $\Delta(q)$ must be a convex function of $q$. Unlike formulations relying on holographic dual forces or spacetime locality, this approach allows us to boldly conjecture that charge spectrum convexity applies to any unitary CFT, extending beyond those with weakly coupled and weakly curved gravitational duals. We term this the Charge Convexity Conjecture and note its generalization to larger global symmetry groups. Testing this via perturbation theory, $1/N$ expansions, and semi-classical methods in examples where anomalous dimensions are calculable confirms the conjecture in all cases examined. However, the underlying CFT reason for this validity remains unclear. Furthermore, unlike the case for global symmetries in AdS (symmetries without a gauge source), violating charge convexity would likely involve a state that can decay into two identical copies with less total energy, thereby breaking unitarity. Consequently, such a violation would constitute an inconsistent feature of the theory. Ultimately, this paper aims to inspire the community to either derive a rigorous proof or identify a counterexample. If the latter occurs, it would demonstrate that unitary CFTs can exhibit non-convex charge dimensions, implying that the weak gravity conjecture lacks a genuine CFT formulation and potentially hiding issues with black hole charge screening or related phenomena. We further explore the conjecture's implications for the swampland, the composite nature of gauge forces in AdS, and the holographic $c$-function. The paper is structured into an introduction, a review of the weak gravity conjecture in AdS/CFT, the introduction of charge convexity as the true underlying principle, technical details on determining anomalous dimensions, and additional discussions on related topics such as the $c$-function, the composite nature of CFT currents, and the monodromy method. Keywords: AdS/CFT Correspondence

novel ancillary services to ensure system security and reliability. Yet, current assessments and policy guidance on market design and ancillary services often fail to account for the intricate interactions between markets and services. To address this gap, this paper introduces an open-source agent-based model designed to evaluate design options for electricity markets and ancillary services. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model (ASAM) integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA toolbox for power system analysis. This model offers adjustable design parameters for both markets and agents, alongside detailed clearing algorithms for day-ahead markets, intra-day continuous trading, redispatch, and imbalances. Additionally, ASAM features extensive policy performance indicators, including new metrics for price mark-ups and redispatch efficiency. A stylized simulation scenario was used to validate the model and explore a specific redispatch design issue. The findings regarding multi-period all-or-none order types in redispatch markets reveal three key implications: (1) The order design minimizes risk for market participants by ensuring full order clearance. (2) Large orders can create dispatch ramps before and after delivery periods, potentially triggering ramp-risk mark-ups and necessitating extra intra-day imbalance trading. (3) In liquid market conditions, an all-or-none design leads to grid operator over-procurement of redispatch because partial order activation is impossible; furthermore, incomplete activation often forces grid operators to introduce system imbalances, as upward and downward redispatch volumes become unequal. These results indicate that, in the absence of market liquidity, all-or-none order designs are unlikely to be the optimal approach for redispatch market design. The validation of this all-or-none mechanism within the simulation demonstrates the model's utility for testing various design alternatives. Consequently, the ASAM tool is recommended for assessing redispatch market designs, particularly in systems with high renewable energy penetration. Introducing a partial fill option to the current all-or-none design could mitigate the over-procurement of redispatch caused by liquid market conditions, provided that risk-based mark-ups are applied correctly. Additionally, the model can support the evaluation of other design options, such as the integration of risk mark-ups or alternative redispatch trading frequencies. The ASAM project will continue to develop and test design proposals relevant to the Dutch context, including the transition to real-time pricing. PyPSA is a versatile tool for power system analysis, and the ASAM model represents a significant advancement by adding dynamic behavior, simulation capabilities, and performance measurement tools. Unlike other models, ASAM uniquely combines dynamic agent-based methods with graph-based PyPSA

This study constrains the formation and dissipation timescales for vortices in both hemispheres, focusing on the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex (NPSV), characterized by higher temperatures and increased hydrocarbon levels at millibar pressures. While the NPSV began forming in late northern spring, it lacked the distinct thermal and compositional contrasts observed at the south pole during its southern summer by the end of Cassini's observations, shortly after the northern summer solstice. The newly formed NPSV was defined by a steepening thermal gradient near $78^\circ$N. Its hexagonal boundary suggests that the Rossby wave responsible for Saturn's persistent polar hexagon—previously thought to remain in the troposphere—can impact stratospheric temperatures roughly 300 km above the cloud tops. We propose that this wave adopts a 'reversed sawtooth' shape, rotating eastward and releasing heat that accounts for the warming signal marking the NPSV's onset. Its dissolution in late summer indicated that the nitrile $\text{C}_2\text{H}_3\text{CN}$ was transported into the previously unlitrified region beyond the NPSV, causing the existing $\text{H}_2\text{CNCO}$ to decline by a factor of three within two Earth months. Consequently, the $^\text{13}\text{CO}_2$ abundance will drop by half by 2020. This two-season cycle is expected to repeat as southern summer approaches, with the southern polar vortex anticipated to emerge from beneath the cold mesopause during its later stages. These cycles will gradually lengthen over the coming centuries, driven by the slow decay of an internal heat source within Saturn.

We demonstrate that solutions possessing negative energy exhibit finite-time blow-up. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is energy-subcritical and given further symmetry constraints, we establish blow-up governed by the same optimal ground-state criterion found in Holmer and Roudenko's work on $\R^{d}$. The traditional Glassey proof, which relies on the concavity of variance, is inapplicable in the presence of an obstacle due to boundary terms arising in the second derivative of the variance that carry an unfavorable sign. To address this, our primary approach involves introducing a novel modified variance that is bounded from below and strictly concave for the specific solutions under consideration. Furthermore, we utilize an explicit example to show that implementing this idea in $\R^{d}$ would result in a contradiction, implying the existence of global, bounded solutions with negative energy and no spatial decay for the Schrödinger equation devoid of an obstacle. An analogous argument by contradiction can be applied to the cubic nonlinearity of the wave equation. The primary innovation of this research lies in the development of the modified variance and the associated analytical techniques. This work extends the findings of [10], which addressed blow-up in the geodesic shadow of an obstacle combined with spatial decay, and [23], which studied initial data close to a bound state for a black hole metric.

Abstract: This paper presents an approach to proving theorems in characteristic-zero commutative algebra using corresponding theorems in positive characteristic. Specifically, we define a class of structures called varieties-with-reductions, which generalize varieties and fibers of flat algebraic schemes. We demonstrate that if a wide variety-with-reductions (encompassing all algebraic complete intersections) has a finite set of associated local reductions, the variety is also tightly (finite set-)parametric. Conversely, for a broad class of varieties-with-reductions, tightness implies the existence of a finite set of local tightly parametric reductions. This characterization allows us to derive the theorem of de Jong and Zariski--Grothendieck from the theorems of Popescu and Tame— respectively. We further characterize Teichmüller space as arising from local tightly parametric reductions and present a Python implementation of the main theorem, accessible at https://andreaswerning.github.io/char0_from_charp/. Although scattered light inherently contains both the amplitude and phase of the electromagnetic field, phase data is frequently discarded during standard intensity measurements. Nevertheless, phase information is often critical for reconstructing target details, a principle established in coherent x-ray imaging. This work presents a novel phase retrieval algorithm capable of recovering field phase data from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra. We demonstrate this technique using x-ray scattering from Mössbauer nuclei at a synchrotron facility. Access to phase data enables a superior reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental results—a level of precision unattainable through conventional methods. Consequently, our approach offers a powerful new tool for data analysis that will advance both x-ray quantum optics and synchrotron-based Mössbauer spectroscopy. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm is broadly applicable to any time and energy resolved spectrum, even when reference beam data is available.

applied to a new hybrid-dimensional model for single-phase Darcy flow in fractured porous media. The model represents fractures as $(d-1)$-dimensional interfaces within a $d$-dimensional domain, where $d$ equals 2 or 3. Fractures are categorized into two types based on the permeability contrast between the fracture and the surrounding matrix: those with significantly higher permeability are termed {\it conductive}, while those with significantly lower permeability are termed {\it blocking}. Conductive fractures are modeled using a standard hybrid-dimensional interface approach assuming continuous pressure across the interface, whereas blocking fractures utilize a recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach that enforces continuity of the normal Darcy velocity component. A key innovation of this scheme is its ability to handle nonconforming meshes regarding blocking fractures, a capability enabled by the Dirac-$\delta$ formulation. Additionally, the numerical method yields locally conservative velocity approximations and generates a symmetric positive definite linear system defined solely on pressure degrees of freedom located at the mesh skeleton. Benchmark tests in both two and three dimensions demonstrate the method's performance, with results showing it to be highly competitive against existing literature approaches. Degree of freedom plots further illustrate the behavior of the proposed scheme relative to other methods across various mesh configurations. Finally, a solution to an inverse problem—estimating the orientations of fracture networks given velocity data from the porous matrix—is used to assess how errors in orientation parameters arise from discretization.

science, with a particular emphasis on hypothesis preference. This preference is typically defined by the difficulty of rejecting a specific hypothesis rather than by the evidence that causes rejection. We introduce the concept of testability as the measure of evidence required to reach a decision based on a given significance level. Alongside hypothesis preference and verifiability (the maximum decision evidence before probability distortion occurs), testability offers another perspective on the evidence needed to make a choice. Like preference and verifiability, testability is inherently tied to the decision process and thus depends on prior probabilities and the cost matrix. Unlike the other two measures, it applies not only to simple hypotheses but also to multiple decision problems involving several hypotheses. Additionally, testability serves as a useful tool in Bayesian analysis for evaluating the efficiency of sample sizes within Bayesian inference. The theoretical foundations of these ideas are grounded in game theory and large deviations theory. Ultimately, this framework provides an efficient method for selecting the sample size necessary to test a specific hypothesis with a designated significance level and a predetermined testability. Although developed within the context of statistical decision making, these principles can be broadly applied across various fields to assist in setting targets for decision evidence when designing experiments or cases, particularly in areas such as cognitive research, legal proceedings, and quality control. The underlying mathematics relies heavily on Markov chains and their absorbing probabilities. An original contribution of this work is the utilization of stochastic verification from large deviations theory to calculate testability across diverse scenarios. The numerical examples presented involve random walks, which serve as models for simple decision problems. Random walks also illustrate key applications in both Bayesian and frequentist analyses. Furthermore, the paper includes a section dedicated to other stochastic processes, demonstrating how to determine testability in such cases. Notably, in a Bayesian setting involving multiple hypotheses, testability aligns with the verification of the most challenging hypothesis to reject. In a frequentist context, however, testability corresponds to the average evidence needed to accept a particular hypothesis. These findings reinforce each other and collectively underscore the practical utility of testability. The paper's mathematical sections offer detailed explanations of the cited principles in the contextual sections. Additionally, the software developed to compute testability and its decision process model is available on GitHub. This tool is designed to help readers investigate the behaviors of diverse decision processes, such as those found in the "Liar or Truth-teller" game. Keywords: hypothesis testing, testability, hypothesis preference, verify, large deviations, bayesian analysis, random walk, markov chain, lie detection, lie catcher, lie tester
